overview.summary: Wildlife biologists study wild animals and their habitats, and work to understand and protect species and ecosystems.
overview.problems: They find out how animal populations are doing, what threatens them and how people and wildlife can share the land.
overview.worksWith: Other scientists, park rangers, local communities, government agencies, conservation groups and landowners.
overview.workplaces: Field sites such as forests, wetlands and parks, laboratories, universities, government agencies and conservation organizations.

timeline.title: Fieldwork
timeline.description: The biologist travels to a site and observes or counts animals, often at dawn when many are active.
timeline.why: Careful counts show whether a population is stable.

timeline.title: Collecting data
timeline.description: The biologist records tracks, signs, camera images or samples using the right permits and methods.

timeline.title: Back at base
timeline.description: The biologist enters data, checks equipment and plans the next visit.

timeline.title: Analysis and reports
timeline.description: The biologist uses statistics and maps to understand patterns and writes reports.

timeline.title: Talking with people
timeline.description: The biologist meets local communities, landowners and agencies about what wildlife needs.
timeline.why: Conservation only works when people cooperate.

timeline.title: Weather and remote travel
timeline.description: Fieldwork may involve long journeys, rough terrain and camping.
timeline.why: Wildlife is often found far from towns.

responsibilities: Planning and carrying out wildlife surveys
Following animal welfare and permit rules
challenges: Fieldwork can be physically demanding, remote and in harsh weather.
Jobs are competitive and often short-term or funded by grants.
Much of the time goes on data and writing, not watching animals.
Pay is low in some roles.
Conservation problems are complex and results can be slow.
Terrain, weather and wild animals bring safety risks.
Postings may be far from home.
workEnvironment: A mix of outdoor field sites, laboratories and offices. Fieldwork can mean early starts, long days and remote locations in all weather. Office work includes data analysis and reports.
tradeoffs: Pay that varies by country and employer

activity.title: Run a 20-minute bird or insect count
steps: With an adult, choose a safe public spot such as a park or school garden.
Sit quietly for 20 minutes and record each kind of bird or insect you see in a table.
Repeat on another day or at another time and compare.
Note one reason your counts might not be complete.
activity.outcome: You practise watching quietly, recording carefully and thinking about the limits of data.
activity.safety: Go with an adult, never touch or chase wild animals, nests or insects that could sting, stay on paths and away from water and roads, and leave nature as you found it.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
